claims.text: Local lattice distortions and chemical short-range order are the primary mediators controlling strength and deformation behavior in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Controlled annealing and quenching treatments can modify chemical short-range order while leaving the overall alloy composition unchanged.
Diffusion is limited during testing at ambient temperature and moderate strain rates.
Having five or more principal elements provides sufficient configurational complexity for the proposed behavior.
Atomic-size variations among alloy components create local lattice distortions.
Variations in bonding energies among alloy components create local lattice distortions.
Increasing chemical short-range order intensifies local stress fields.
The local stress fields associated with lattice distortion and chemical short-range order impede dislocation motion.
The local stress fields associated with lattice distortion and chemical short-range order modify slip mechanisms.
Impeded dislocation motion caused by these local stress fields increases yield strength.
Changes in local stress fields and slip mechanisms alter ductility.
Specimens with increased short-range order should have higher yield strength than near-random specimens of the same composition.
Specimens with increased short-range order should exhibit fewer or narrower slip bands than near-random baseline specimens.
Rapid quenching produces a near-random atomic distribution and minimizes chemical short-range order.
The proposed effect should hold when configurational complexity is high enough for lattice distortion and short-range order to dominate the mechanical response.
The proposed effect should hold under deformation conditions that do not promote extensive dynamic recovery or recrystallization.
